notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Soil is the uppermost weathered layer of the Earth's crust that supports plant growth.
  • It contains:
  • Mineral particles.
  • Organic matter.
  • Water.
  • Air.
  • Living organisms.
  • Soil develops slowly through the interaction of rock, climate, organisms, relief and time.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Soil → Weathered Rock + Organic Matter + Water + Air

2. Soil Formation

Soil formation is called pedogenesis.

Major soil-forming factors include:

  • Parent material.
  • Climate.
  • Relief.
  • Organisms.
  • Time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Soil Formation → Parent Rock + Climate + Relief + Organisms + Time

3. Parent Material
  • Parent material is the rock or sediment from which soil develops.
  • It strongly influences:
  • Mineral composition.
  • Texture.
  • Colour.
  • Fertility.
4. Climate and Soil Formation

Climate affects:

  • Weathering.
  • Leaching.
  • Organic-matter decomposition.
  • Soil moisture.
  • Chemical reactions.
  • High rainfall increases leaching.
  • Dry climates favour accumulation of salts and calcium compounds.
5. Relief and Soil
  • Steep slopes generally have thin soils because erosion is strong.
  • Plains and valleys often have deeper soils due to deposition.
  • Slope direction also affects moisture and vegetation.
6. Organisms and Soil

Plants, animals and microorganisms:

  • Add organic matter.
  • Decompose residues.
  • Mix soil.
  • Recycle nutrients.
  • Influence soil structure.
7. Time
  • Mature soils generally require long periods to develop.
  • Younger soils show less-developed horizons.
  • River alluvium may be periodically renewed and remain comparatively young.
8. Soil Profile

A vertical section through soil is called a soil profile.

It contains distinct layers called horizons.

9. Major Soil Horizons

Common horizons include:

  • O Horizon.
  • A Horizon.
  • E Horizon.
  • B Horizon.
  • C Horizon.
  • R Horizon.

Not every soil contains all horizons clearly.

10. O Horizon
  • O horizon consists mainly of organic litter and decomposing plant material.
  • It is common in forest soils.
11. A Horizon
  • A horizon is commonly called topsoil.
  • It contains mineral material mixed with humus.
  • It is usually the most biologically active mineral layer.
📌 Must-Memorise

A Horizon → Topsoil

12. E Horizon
  • E horizon is a zone of strong leaching or eluviation.
  • Clay, iron and organic matter may be removed from this layer.
  • It is not prominent in every soil.
13. B Horizon
  • B horizon is commonly called subsoil.
  • Materials removed from upper layers may accumulate here.
  • Clay, iron or aluminium compounds can become concentrated.
📌 Must-Memorise

B Horizon → Subsoil / Accumulation Zone

14. C Horizon
  • C horizon consists mainly of partly weathered parent material.
  • Soil-forming processes are weaker here than in upper layers.
15. R Horizon
  • R horizon represents relatively unweathered bedrock beneath the soil.
16. Humus
  • Humus is dark, decomposed organic matter in soil.
  • It improves:
  • Soil structure.
  • Water retention.
  • Nutrient-holding capacity.
  • Humus is produced through decomposition of plant and animal remains.
17. Soil Texture

Soil texture depends on the relative proportions of:

  • Sand.
  • Silt.
  • Clay.
18. Sand
  • Sand particles are relatively large.
  • Sandy soils have:
  • Large pore spaces.
  • Rapid drainage.
  • Lower water retention.
19. Clay
  • Clay particles are very fine.
  • Clay-rich soils generally have:
  • High water-holding capacity.
  • Small pore spaces.
  • Slower drainage.
20. Silt
  • Silt particles are intermediate between sand and clay in size.
  • Silt-rich soils can be fertile but may be easily eroded.
21. Loam
  • Loam contains a favourable mixture of sand, silt and clay.
  • It combines:
  • Good drainage.
  • Good moisture retention.
  • Suitable aeration.
  • Loamy soils are generally favourable for agriculture.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Loam → Balanced Soil Texture

22. Soil Structure
  • Soil structure refers to the arrangement of soil particles into aggregates.
  • Good structure improves:
  • Aeration.
  • Root penetration.
  • Water infiltration.
23. Soil Porosity
  • Porosity is the proportion of pore spaces in soil.
  • Pores hold air and water.
  • Soil texture and structure influence porosity.
24. Soil Permeability
  • Permeability refers to the ability of soil to allow water to move through it.
  • Sandy soils are generally more permeable than clay-rich soils.
25. Soil pH
  • Soil pH measures acidity or alkalinity.
  • pH below 7 → Acidic.
  • pH 7 → Neutral.
  • pH above 7 → Alkaline.
📌 Must-Memorise

pH < 7 → Acidic

pH > 7 → Alkaline

26. Soil Fertility
  • Soil fertility is the ability of soil to provide essential nutrients to plants.
  • Fertility depends on:
  • Nutrient content.
  • pH.
  • Organic matter.
  • Water.
  • Soil structure.
27. Major Soil Types of India

The major soil groups commonly studied in Indian geography are:

  • Alluvial soil.
  • Black soil.
  • Red and yellow soil.
  • Laterite soil.
  • Arid/desert soil.
  • Forest and mountain soil.
  • Saline and alkaline soil.
  • Peaty and marshy soil.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India → Diverse Soils Because of Diverse Geology + Climate + Relief

28. Alluvial Soil — Overview
  • Alluvial soil is the most widespread and agriculturally important soil group in India.
  • It is formed by deposition of sediments carried by rivers.
  • It dominates the Northern Plains.
  • It also occurs in river valleys and coastal deltas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Most Widespread Indian Soil → Alluvial

29. Distribution of Alluvial Soil

Major regions include:

  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Bihar.
  • West Bengal.
  • Assam plains.
  • Coastal and deltaic plains of major east-flowing rivers.
  • Parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan river plains.
30. Composition of Alluvial Soil

Alluvial soil contains varying proportions of:

  • Sand.
  • Silt.
  • Clay.

Its texture changes according to location and depositional environment.

31. Fertility of Alluvial Soil
  • Alluvial soils are generally fertile.
  • They commonly contain adequate:
  • Potash.
  • Lime.
  • Phosphoric compounds in varying amounts.
  • Nitrogen and humus may be relatively deficient in many areas.
32. Crops in Alluvial Soil

Major crops include:

  • Rice.
  • Wheat.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Maize.
  • Pulses.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Jute.
33. Bhangar
  • Bhangar is older alluvial soil.
  • It occurs on slightly elevated terraces.
  • It is generally above the active floodplain.
  • It may contain kankar nodules.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhangar → Old Alluvium

34. Khadar
  • Khadar is newer alluvial soil.
  • It occurs in active floodplains.
  • It is periodically renewed by river floods.
  • It is generally highly fertile.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khadar → New Alluvium

35. Kankar
  • Kankar refers to calcareous concretions or nodules.
  • It is commonly associated with Bhangar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhangar → Kankar

36. Bhangar vs Khadar

Bhangar:

  • Older.
  • Higher terrace.
  • Less frequently flooded.
  • Kankar common.

Khadar:

  • Newer.
  • Lower floodplain.
  • Renewed by floods.
  • More agriculturally productive in many places.
37. Alluvial Soil in Deltas

Major delta regions include:

  • Mahanadi.
  • Godavari.
  • Krishna.
  • Kaveri.

These contain fine alluvial deposits and support intensive agriculture.

38. Tamil Nadu Alluvial Soil

In Tamil Nadu, alluvial soils occur mainly in:

  • River valleys.
  • Kaveri delta.
  • Tamiraparani basin.
  • Vaigai and other river plains.
  • Coastal lowlands.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Kaveri Delta → Fertile Alluvial Soil

39. Black Soil — Overview
  • Black soil is one of India's major soil types.
  • It is strongly associated with the Deccan Trap region.
  • It develops largely from basaltic rocks.
  • It is also called regur soil.
  • It is famous for cotton cultivation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Black Soil = Regur = Cotton Soil

40. Origin of Black Soil
  • Black soil develops from weathering of basaltic lava rocks in large parts of the Deccan Plateau.
  • It contains large amounts of clay.
41. Distribution of Black Soil

Major regions include:

  • Maharashtra.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Gujarat.
  • Telangana.
  • Parts of Karnataka.
  • Parts of Andhra Pradesh.
  • Smaller areas in Tamil Nadu.
42. Properties of Black Soil

Black soil generally has:

  • High clay content.
  • High moisture-retention capacity.
  • Low permeability.
  • Strong swelling when wet.
  • Shrinkage and cracking when dry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Black Soil → Swells Wet + Cracks Dry

43. Self-Ploughing Nature
  • Deep cracks develop in black soil during the dry season.
  • These cracks help aerate and loosen the soil.
  • Therefore, black soil is sometimes described as self-ploughing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Black Soil → Self-Ploughing

44. Nutrient Characteristics of Black Soil

Black soil is generally rich in:

  • Calcium carbonate.
  • Magnesium.
  • Potash.
  • Lime.

It may be relatively deficient in:

  • Nitrogen.
  • Phosphorus.
  • Organic matter.
45. Cotton and Black Soil
  • Black soil retains moisture for a long period.
  • This suits cotton cultivation.
  • Cotton's deep roots can use stored soil moisture.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Black Soil → Cotton

46. Other Crops in Black Soil

Crops include:

  • Cotton.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Wheat.
  • Groundnut.
  • Tobacco.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Pulses.
47. Black Soil in Tamil Nadu

Black soil occurs in parts of:

  • Coimbatore region.
  • Erode region.
  • Tiruppur.
  • Thoothukudi.
  • Virudhunagar.
  • Tirunelveli and adjoining interior areas in varying patches.

It supports cotton and other dryland crops.

48. Red Soil — Overview
  • Red soil is widespread over the Peninsular Plateau.
  • It develops mainly from weathering of ancient crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks.
  • Its red colour is due largely to iron oxides.
📌 Must-Memorise

Red Soil Colour → Iron Oxide

49. Distribution of Red Soil

Major regions include:

  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Karnataka.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Telangana.
  • Odisha.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Jharkhand.
  • Parts of Madhya Pradesh.
  • Eastern Maharashtra.
50. Red and Yellow Soil
  • Red soils may appear yellow when iron compounds occur in a hydrated form.
  • Therefore, many classifications group them as red and yellow soils.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Red/Yellow Colour → Forms of Iron Compounds

51. Properties of Red Soil

Red soils are generally:

  • Porous.
  • Well drained.
  • Low in humus.
  • Low in nitrogen.
  • Low in phosphorus.
  • Variable in fertility.
52. Fertility Improvement of Red Soil

Productivity can be improved using:

  • Irrigation.
  • Manure.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Organic matter.
  • Soil conservation.
53. Crops in Red Soil

Common crops include:

  • Millets.
  • Groundnut.
  • Pulses.
  • Cotton.
  • Tobacco.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Some rice under irrigation.
54. Tamil Nadu and Red Soil
  • Red soil is one of the most widespread soil groups in Tamil Nadu.
  • It occurs extensively across interior and upland districts.
  • Its agricultural productivity depends strongly on rainfall and irrigation.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Red Soil Widespread

55. Laterite Soil — Overview
  • Laterite soil develops under conditions of high temperature and heavy rainfall.
  • Intense leaching removes soluble materials.
  • Iron and aluminium compounds become concentrated.
📌 Must-Memorise

Laterite → Heavy Rainfall + Strong Leaching

56. Meaning of Laterite
  • The word laterite is associated with the Latin word later, meaning brick.
  • Laterite can harden on exposure to air.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Laterite → Brick-Like Hardening

57. Leaching
  • Leaching is the removal of soluble minerals from upper soil layers by downward-moving water.
  • Heavy rainfall accelerates leaching.
58. Distribution of Laterite Soil

Important areas include:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Parts of Karnataka.
  • Kerala.
  • Tamil Nadu highlands.
  • Odisha.
  • Assam and northeastern uplands.
  • Parts of Maharashtra.
59. Properties of Laterite Soil

Laterite soils are often:

  • Acidic.
  • Low in humus.
  • Low in nitrogen.
  • Low in phosphate.
  • Rich in iron and aluminium oxides.
60. Crops in Laterite Soil

With suitable manure and irrigation, crops include:

  • Tea.
  • Coffee.
  • Rubber.
  • Cashew.
  • Coconut in suitable regions.
61. Laterite in Tamil Nadu

Lateritic soils occur in parts of:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Nilgiri region.
  • High-rainfall uplands.
  • Some coastal and hill tracts.
62. Arid Soil — Overview
  • Arid soils occur mainly in western Rajasthan and adjoining dry regions.
  • They form under low rainfall and high evaporation.
  • They are generally sandy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Arid Soil → Rajasthan

63. Properties of Arid Soil

Arid soil typically has:

  • Sandy texture.
  • Low humus.
  • Low moisture.
  • High soluble salt content in some areas.
  • Calcium carbonate accumulation in lower horizons.
64. Kankar in Arid Soil
  • Calcium carbonate can accumulate below the surface.
  • This may form a kankar layer.
  • Such layers can reduce water infiltration.
65. Irrigation and Arid Soil
  • With irrigation, desert soils can become productive.
  • However, poor drainage may cause:
  • Salinity.
  • Waterlogging.
66. Crops in Arid Soil

Common crops include:

  • Bajra.
  • Pulses.
  • Mustard.
  • Wheat and cotton under irrigation.
67. Forest and Mountain Soils
  • Forest and mountain soils occur in hilly and mountainous regions.
  • Their characteristics vary greatly with:
  • Altitude.
  • Rainfall.
  • Vegetation.
  • Slope.
68. Himalayan Mountain Soils
  • Valley soils may be deep and fertile.
  • Steep slopes have thin immature soils.
  • Higher areas contain coarse and stony soils.
  • Forest litter increases organic matter in many zones.
69. Acidic Mountain Soils
  • High rainfall and leaching can make mountain soils acidic.
  • Tea grows well in acidic soils under suitable climatic conditions.
70. Plantation Crops in Mountain Soils

Important crops include:

  • Tea.
  • Coffee.
  • Spices.
  • Temperate fruits in cooler zones.
71. Saline Soil — Overview
  • Saline soils contain excessive soluble salts.
  • They occur especially in:
  • Arid regions.
  • Poorly drained irrigated areas.
  • Coastal regions.
72. Causes of Soil Salinity

Causes include:

  • High evaporation.
  • Poor drainage.
  • Excess irrigation.
  • Saline groundwater.
  • Seawater intrusion.
  • Coastal flooding.
73. Saline Soil in Coastal Tamil Nadu
  • Coastal areas can experience salinity because of:
  • Seawater intrusion.
  • Cyclone-induced inundation.
  • Poor drainage.
  • Groundwater over-extraction can worsen coastal salinity.
74. Alkaline Soil
  • Alkaline soils have high pH.
  • Sodium compounds may accumulate.
  • Poor soil structure and reduced infiltration can occur.
75. Reh / Usar Soil
  • Saline and alkaline soils are locally called by names such as reh, usar or kallar in different regions.
  • These soils require reclamation for productive agriculture.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Usar/Reh → Saline-Alkaline Soil

76. Reclamation of Alkaline Soil

Methods include:

  • Gypsum application.
  • Improved drainage.
  • Leaching of salts.
  • Organic matter addition.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sodic/Alkaline Soil → Gypsum

77. Acid Soil Reclamation
  • Lime is commonly applied to acidic soils.
  • It helps raise soil pH.
📌 Must-Memorise

Acidic Soil → Lime

Alkaline/Sodic Soil → Gypsum

78. Peaty Soil
  • Peaty soils contain large amounts of organic matter.
  • They form in waterlogged conditions where decomposition is slow.
  • They may be acidic.
79. Distribution of Peaty and Marshy Soils

They occur in parts of:

  • Kerala.
  • Sundarbans.
  • Coastal and deltaic marshes.
  • Some wetland regions of Bihar and Odisha.
80. Marshy Soil
  • Marshy soils remain waterlogged for long periods.
  • They contain high organic matter but may require drainage for agriculture.
81. Kari Soil
  • Dark peaty soils in parts of Kerala are locally known as kari soils.
  • They occur in low-lying waterlogged regions.
82. Soil Erosion — Basic Meaning
  • Soil erosion is the removal of the fertile upper layer of soil.
  • It is caused by:
  • Water.
  • Wind.
  • Human activities.
  • Excessive erosion lowers agricultural productivity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Most Fertile Layer Lost → Topsoil

83. Natural vs Accelerated Erosion

Natural erosion:

  • Occurs slowly under natural processes.

Accelerated erosion:

  • Occurs rapidly because of human disturbance such as deforestation and poor land management.
84. Major Causes of Soil Erosion
  • Deforestation.
  • Overgrazing.
  • Shifting cultivation.
  • Excessive ploughing.
  • Improper irrigation.
  • Mining.
  • Construction.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Strong winds.
85. Water Erosion

Major forms include:

  • Splash erosion.
  • Sheet erosion.
  • Rill erosion.
  • Gully erosion.
86. Splash Erosion
  • Raindrops strike exposed soil.
  • Soil particles are detached and displaced.
  • It is the first stage of water erosion.
87. Sheet Erosion
  • A thin, relatively uniform layer of soil is removed over a wide area.
  • It may be difficult to notice initially.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sheet Erosion → Uniform Thin Layer Removed

88. Rill Erosion
  • Small channels called rills develop as runoff concentrates.
  • Rills may be removed temporarily by ploughing.
89. Gully Erosion
  • Large channels develop when rills deepen and widen.
  • Land can become unsuitable for cultivation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gully Erosion → Deep Channels

90. Chambal Ravines
  • Severe gully erosion has created ravines along the Chambal basin.
  • These landscapes are often called badlands.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chambal → Gully Erosion → Ravines

91. Wind Erosion
  • Wind erosion is important in arid and semi-arid regions.
  • Loose dry soil particles are lifted and transported.
  • Rajasthan and adjoining dry regions are particularly vulnerable.
92. Deflation
  • Deflation is removal of loose fine soil particles by wind.
93. Soil Deposition by Wind
  • Wind may deposit transported material when velocity decreases.
  • Sand dunes and fine dust deposits can result.
94. Desertification and Soil
  • Desertification is land degradation in dry regions.
  • Soil erosion, vegetation loss and salinity are major contributors.
95. Soil Conservation

Soil conservation aims to:

  • Reduce erosion.
  • Maintain fertility.
  • Improve water infiltration.
  • Protect vegetation.
  • Sustain agricultural productivity.
96. Contour Ploughing
  • Ploughing is done along contour lines rather than up and down slopes.
  • It slows runoff.
  • It reduces soil erosion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Contour Ploughing → Across Slope

97. Contour Bunding
  • Small embankments are constructed along contour lines.
  • They slow water movement.
  • They increase infiltration.
98. Terrace Farming
  • Steep slopes are converted into step-like fields.
  • Terraces reduce runoff velocity.
  • They are common in mountain regions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Terracing → Mountain Soil Conservation

99. Strip Cropping
  • Different crops are planted in alternating strips.
  • Strips reduce wind and water erosion.
  • It is useful on gently sloping or windy land.
100. Shelterbelts
  • Rows of trees are planted across prevailing wind direction.
  • They reduce wind velocity.
  • They help control wind erosion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shelterbelt → Wind Erosion Control

101. Afforestation
  • Planting trees protects soil from:
  • Raindrop impact.
  • Wind.
  • Surface runoff.
  • Roots bind the soil.
102. Controlled Grazing
  • Overgrazing removes protective vegetation.
  • Controlled grazing allows vegetation recovery.
  • It reduces erosion in grasslands and dry regions.
103. Check Dams
  • Small barriers across gullies slow runoff.
  • They trap sediments.
  • They help stabilise eroded land.
104. Mulching
  • Organic or synthetic material is placed over the soil surface.
  • It reduces:
  • Evaporation.
  • Soil erosion.
  • Weed growth.
105. Crop Rotation
  • Different crops are grown in sequence.
  • Crop rotation helps maintain soil fertility.
  • Legumes can increase soil nitrogen through biological fixation.
106. Legumes and Nitrogen
  • Leguminous plants often contain Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules.
  • Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Legume Root Nodules → Rhizobium

107. Green Manuring
  • Green crops are grown and incorporated into soil.
  • They add organic matter and nutrients.
  • Leguminous green-manure crops can improve nitrogen status.
108. Organic Manure

Examples include:

  • Farmyard manure.
  • Compost.
  • Green manure.
  • Vermicompost.

They improve soil structure and organic matter.

109. Chemical Fertilisers and Soil
  • Fertilisers provide nutrients quickly.
  • Excessive or imbalanced use may cause:
  • Soil acidification.
  • Nutrient imbalance.
  • Water pollution.
  • Balanced nutrient management is preferable.
110. Integrated Nutrient Management
  • Integrated nutrient management combines:
  • Chemical fertilisers.
  • Organic manure.
  • Biofertilisers.
  • It aims to maintain productivity and soil health.
111. Soil Organic Carbon
  • Soil organic carbon is stored in soil organic matter.
  • It improves:
  • Fertility.
  • Water retention.
  • Structure.
  • Soils also act as major carbon stores.
112. Soil Moisture
  • Soil moisture is water stored in soil pores.
  • It is essential for plant growth.
  • Texture, organic matter and rainfall influence storage.
113. Field Capacity
  • Field capacity is the amount of water retained in soil after excess gravitational water drains away.
  • It represents a favourable moisture condition for plants.
114. Wilting Point
  • Permanent wilting point is the soil-moisture level below which plants cannot extract enough water to recover from wilting.
115. Available Water
  • Plant-available water is broadly the moisture held between field capacity and permanent wilting point.
116. Black Soil and Water Holding
  • Black soil has high clay content.
  • Therefore, it has high water-holding capacity.
  • This helps crops withstand dry periods.
117. Sandy Soil and Water Holding
  • Sandy soil drains rapidly.
  • It retains comparatively little water.
  • Crops may require more frequent irrigation.
118. Clay Soil and Drainage
  • Clay-rich soil retains more moisture.
  • Poor structure can cause slow drainage and waterlogging.
119. Soil Salinisation
  • Salinisation is accumulation of soluble salts in soil.
  • It is common in:
  • Arid climates.
  • Irrigated areas with poor drainage.
  • Coastal regions.
120. Soil Sodicity
  • Sodic soils contain excessive exchangeable sodium.
  • Soil structure becomes poor.
  • Infiltration and drainage decline.
121. Leaching as Reclamation
  • In saline soils, good-quality water can be used to wash soluble salts downward.
  • Adequate drainage is essential.
122. Waterlogging and Soil Degradation
  • Persistent waterlogging reduces oxygen in the root zone.
  • It can increase salinity in dry regions.
  • Crop growth is affected.
123. Soil Acidification

Soil may become acidic because of:

  • Heavy rainfall and leaching.
  • Certain fertilisers.
  • Natural parent material.

Lime can be used to reduce acidity.

124. Laterisation
  • Laterisation is intense weathering and leaching under warm, wet tropical conditions.
  • Silica and bases are removed.
  • Iron and aluminium oxides become concentrated.
📌 Must-Memorise

Laterisation → Strong Tropical Leaching

125. Calcification
  • Calcification is accumulation of calcium compounds in soil.
  • It occurs more commonly under dry conditions where evaporation exceeds rainfall.
126. Podzolisation — Concept
  • Podzolisation involves strong leaching under cool, humid forest conditions.
  • Upper horizons become depleted.
  • It is more important in colder mountain environments than in tropical lowlands.
127. Soil Colour

Soil colour can indicate:

  • Iron compounds.
  • Organic matter.
  • Drainage conditions.
  • Parent material.

Examples:

  • Red → Iron oxide.
  • Black → Clay/mineral and organic characteristics of basalt-derived soils.
  • Dark brown/black → Often higher organic matter in some soils.
128. Soil Testing

Soil testing helps determine:

  • pH.
  • Nutrient status.
  • Salinity.
  • Organic matter.
  • Fertiliser requirement.
129. Soil Health

Healthy soil should have:

  • Good structure.
  • Adequate organic matter.
  • Balanced nutrients.
  • Suitable pH.
  • Good microbial activity.
  • Proper drainage.
130. Soil and Agriculture

Soil type influences:

  • Crop selection.
  • Irrigation need.
  • Fertiliser requirement.
  • Root development.
  • Yield.
131. Major Soil–Crop Associations
  • Alluvial → Rice, wheat, sugarcane, jute.
  • Black → Cotton.
  • Red → Groundnut, millets, pulses.
  • Laterite → Tea, coffee, rubber, cashew with management.
  • Arid → Bajra and drought-resistant crops.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Soil ↔ Crop Matching

132. Soil and Natural Vegetation
  • Deep fertile soils support dense vegetation if rainfall is adequate.
  • Thin mountain soils support sparse vegetation at high altitude.
  • Desert soils support thorn scrub.
  • Lateritic high-rainfall regions support tropical vegetation where undisturbed.
133. Tamil Nadu — Major Soil Groups

Tamil Nadu has important areas of:

  • Red soil.
  • Black soil.
  • Alluvial soil.
  • Laterite soil.
  • Coastal saline soil.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Most Widespread TN Soil → Red Soil

134. Tamil Nadu Red Soil Regions

Red soils occur widely across:

  • Northern interior districts.
  • Central uplands.
  • Southern interior regions.
  • Eastern Ghats and adjoining plains.
135. Tamil Nadu Black Soil Regions

Black soils are important in parts of:

  • Coimbatore.
  • Tiruppur.
  • Erode.
  • Virudhunagar.
  • Thoothukudi.
  • Tirunelveli region.

These areas support cotton and dryland agriculture.

136. Tamil Nadu Alluvial Soil Regions

Alluvial soils are particularly important in:

  • Kaveri delta.
  • Tamiraparani valley.
  • Vaigai basin.
  • Palar and Ponnaiyar river plains.
  • Coastal river valleys.
137. Kaveri Delta Soil
  • Kaveri delta contains fertile alluvial soils.
  • Paddy is the dominant crop.
  • Irrigation and river deposition historically supported intensive agriculture.
138. Tamil Nadu Laterite Soil

Laterite soils occur in:

  • Nilgiris.
  • Western Ghats.
  • High-rainfall hill regions.
  • Selected upland areas.
139. Tamil Nadu Coastal Salinity

Coastal soil salinity is significant in some low-lying areas because of:

  • Seawater intrusion.
  • Poor drainage.
  • Cyclonic inundation.
  • High evaporation.
140. Soil Erosion in Tamil Nadu

Important vulnerable regions include:

  • Western Ghats.
  • Nilgiris.
  • Eastern Ghats.
  • Dry southern districts.
  • Coastal sand-dune regions.
141. Nilgiri Soil Erosion
  • Steep slopes and intense rainfall increase erosion risk.
  • Landslides may remove large volumes of soil.
  • Vegetation removal increases vulnerability.
142. Dryland Soil Conservation in Tamil Nadu

Useful measures include:

  • Contour bunding.
  • Farm ponds.
  • Check dams.
  • Mulching.
  • Drought-resistant crops.
  • Shelterbelts.
143. Coastal Sand Stabilisation
  • Vegetation can stabilise coastal dunes.
  • Plant roots reduce wind erosion.
  • Dune protection also helps reduce coastal vulnerability.
144. Soil Degradation

Soil degradation includes:

  • Erosion.
  • Salinity.
  • Sodicity.
  • Acidification.
  • Nutrient depletion.
  • Waterlogging.
  • Compaction.
  • Contamination.
145. Soil Compaction
  • Compaction occurs when soil particles are pressed together.
  • It reduces pore space.
  • Heavy machinery and repeated trampling can cause it.
  • Root growth and infiltration decline.
146. Soil Contamination

Soils may be polluted by:

  • Heavy metals.
  • Industrial waste.
  • Excess pesticides.
  • Petroleum products.
  • Solid waste.
  • Sewage sludge.
147. Desertification and Land Degradation
  • Desertification does not simply mean expansion of existing deserts.
  • It means degradation of dryland productivity.
  • It can occur through:
  • Erosion.
  • Salinity.
  • Vegetation loss.
  • Unsustainable land use.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Desertification ≠ Only Desert Expansion

148. Land Capability
  • Land capability refers to the suitability of land for different uses without causing long-term degradation.
  • Soil, slope, erosion risk and climate are important factors.
149. Sustainable Soil Management

Key principles include:

  • Maintain vegetation cover.
  • Reduce erosion.
  • Add organic matter.
  • Use balanced fertilisers.
  • Avoid over-irrigation.
  • Protect soil biodiversity.
  • Match crops with soil capability.
150. Important Soil Terms
  • Pedogenesis → Soil formation.
  • Humus → Decomposed organic matter.
  • Leaching → Downward removal of soluble minerals.
  • Eluviation → Removal from an upper horizon.
  • Illuviation → Accumulation in a lower horizon.
  • Salinisation → Salt accumulation.
  • Laterisation → Intense tropical leaching.
  • Soil profile → Vertical soil section.
151. Eluviation
  • Eluviation means removal of fine particles or dissolved substances from an upper soil horizon.
  • The E horizon is often an eluviation zone.
152. Illuviation
  • Illuviation means deposition or accumulation of materials transported from upper soil layers.
  • The B horizon is commonly an accumulation zone.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

E Horizon → Eluviation

B Horizon → Illuviation

153. Soil Conservation and Watershed Management
  • Soil and water conservation are closely linked.
  • Slowing runoff:
  • Reduces erosion.
  • Increases infiltration.
  • Improves groundwater recharge.
  • Watershed management therefore protects both land and water.
154. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Alluvial → Northern Plains.
  • Bhangar → Old alluvium.
  • Khadar → New alluvium.
  • Bhangar → Kankar.
  • Black → Regur.
  • Black → Cotton.
  • Black → Basalt.
  • Red → Iron oxide.
  • Laterite → Leaching.
  • Arid → Rajasthan.
  • Acid soil → Lime.
  • Sodic soil → Gypsum.
  • Chambal → Ravines.
  • Contour ploughing → Water erosion control.
  • Shelterbelt → Wind erosion control.
  • Terrace farming → Hills.
  • Tamil Nadu → Red soil widespread.
  • Kaveri Delta → Alluvial.
  • Coimbatore region → Black soil patches.
  • Nilgiris → Laterite/mountain soils.
155. TNPSC Traps
  • Soil is not only broken rock; it also contains organic matter, air, water and organisms.
  • Pedogenesis means soil formation.
  • A horizon is topsoil.
  • B horizon is subsoil/accumulation zone.
  • C horizon is weathered parent material.
  • Alluvial soil is the most widespread soil in India.
  • Bhangar is older alluvium.
  • Khadar is newer alluvium.
  • Kankar is associated with Bhangar.
  • Black soil is also called regur.
  • Black soil is strongly associated with Deccan basalt.
  • Black soil swells when wet and cracks when dry.
  • Black soil is famous for cotton.
  • Red soil colour is due mainly to iron oxides.
  • Red soil is widespread in Tamil Nadu.
  • Laterite develops under high temperature and heavy rainfall.
  • Laterite formation involves intense leaching.
  • Arid soil is common in Rajasthan.
  • Saline soil and alkaline soil are not exactly the same.
  • Gypsum is used mainly for sodic/alkaline soil reclamation.
  • Lime is used for acidic soils.
  • Peaty soil is rich in organic matter.
  • Sheet erosion removes a thin layer.
  • Gully erosion creates deep channels.
  • Chambal ravines result from severe gully erosion.
  • Shelterbelts reduce wind erosion.
  • Contour ploughing reduces runoff.
  • Terracing is suited to slopes.
  • Over-irrigation can cause salinity and waterlogging.
  • Coastal groundwater extraction can contribute to soil and water salinity.
  • Desertification does not mean only expansion of sand dunes.
156. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Soil formation → Pedogenesis.
  • A horizon → Topsoil.
  • B horizon → Subsoil.
  • C → Parent material.
  • Alluvial → Most widespread.
  • Bhangar → Old.
  • Khadar → New.
  • Black → Regur.
  • Black → Cotton.
  • Black → Basalt.
  • Red → Iron.
  • Tamil Nadu → Red soil.
  • Laterite → Leaching.
  • Arid → Rajasthan.
  • Acid → Lime.
  • Sodic → Gypsum.
  • Peaty → Organic matter.
  • Sheet → Thin layer.
  • Gully → Deep channels.
  • Chambal → Ravines.
  • Terrace → Hills.
  • Shelterbelt → Wind.
  • Contour → Water erosion.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Five major soil-forming factors? → Parent material, climate, relief, organisms and time.
  • What is a soil profile? → Vertical section showing soil horizons.
  • Topsoil horizon? → A horizon.
  • Subsoil horizon? → B horizon.
  • Partly weathered parent material? → C horizon.
  • Bedrock horizon? → R horizon.
  • Organic surface layer? → O horizon.
  • What is humus? → Decomposed organic matter.
  • Main soil-texture components? → Sand, silt and clay.
  • Which particle is largest? → Sand.
  • Which is finest? → Clay.
  • Balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay? → Loam.
  • Soil pH below 7 means? → Acidic.
  • Soil pH above 7 means? → Alkaline.
  • Most widespread soil of India? → Alluvial soil.
  • Alluvial soil formed by? → River deposition.
  • Main region of alluvial soil? → Northern Plains.
  • Older alluvium? → Bhangar.
  • Newer alluvium? → Khadar.
  • Which contains kankar? → Bhangar.
  • Which is renewed by floods? → Khadar.
  • Major alluvial crops? → Rice, wheat, sugarcane and jute.
  • Black soil is also called? → Regur.
  • Black soil developed mainly from? → Basaltic Deccan Trap rocks.
  • Main crop associated with black soil? → Cotton.
  • Why is black soil called self-ploughing? → It cracks deeply during dry periods.
  • Main property of black soil? → High moisture retention.
  • Red soil colour is due to? → Iron oxides.
  • Which Indian state has widespread red soil important for TNPSC? → Tamil Nadu.
  • Laterite soil forms under? → High temperature and heavy rainfall.
  • Main process in laterite formation? → Intense leaching.
  • Laterite is rich in? → Iron and aluminium compounds.

  • What is eluviation? → Removal of materials from an upper soil horizon.
  • What is illuviation? → Accumulation of materials in a lower horizon.

  • Which commonly shows illuviation? → B horizon.
  • What is sheet erosion? → Uniform removal of a thin soil layer.
  • What is gully erosion? → Formation of deep erosion channels.
  • Famous Indian ravine region? → Chambal basin.
  • What is contour ploughing? → Ploughing along contour lines to reduce runoff.
  • Main method used on steep mountain slopes? → Terrace farming.

  • Which material is used to reclaim sodic/alkaline soil? → Gypsum.
  • Which material is used to correct acidic soil? → Lime.
  • What is laterisation? → Intense tropical weathering and leaching that concentrates iron and aluminium.
  • What is calcification? → Accumulation of calcium compounds under relatively dry conditions.
  • Major soils of Tamil Nadu? → Red, black, alluvial, laterite and coastal saline soils.
  • Most widespread soil of Tamil Nadu? → Red soil.
  • Main soil of Kaveri delta? → Alluvial soil.
  • Important soil associated with cotton areas of western/southern Tamil Nadu? → Black soil.
  • Why are Nilgiris vulnerable to soil erosion? → Steep slopes and heavy rainfall.
  • What is soil compaction? → Compression of soil reducing pore space.
  • What is desertification? → Land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions.
  • Is desertification only the spread of an existing desert? → No.
